items.reasoning: Take R's salary as 100. Then Q = 80% of 100 = 80, and P = 80% of 80 = 64. R exceeds P by 100 − 64 = 36, and the excess is expressed as a percentage of P, the base named in the question: 36/64 × 100 = 56·25%. (The tempting 36% is the excess measured against R, which the stem does not ask for.)

The intended result is 4x and the mistaken result is x/4. The change is (x/4 − 4x)/(4x) = (0·25 − 4)/4 = −0·9375, i.e. a fall of 93·75% from the correct value. Equivalently the wrong answer is only 1/16 of the right one, so 15/16 = 93·75% of it has been lost.

20% failed English and 30% failed Hindi, while 15% failed both. By inclusion–exclusion, those failing at least one subject are 20 + 30 − 15 = 35%. Removing the 15% who failed both leaves 35 − 15 = 20% who failed in exactly one subject (5% in English only and 15% in Hindi only).

Let the present ages be F and S. 'n years back I was as old as you are now' gives F − n = S, so n = F − S. 'My present age is four times your age n years back' gives F = 4(S − n) = 4(2S − F), hence 5F = 8S. With F + S = 130 this yields S = 50 and F = 80, a difference of 30. Checking: n = 30, the son was 20 thirty years ago, and 4 × 20 = 80 = the father's present age.

One litre is 1000 cm³, and 1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³, so 1000 litres = 1 m³ — statement 1 is correct. A metric ton (tonne) is by definition 1000 kg — statement 2 is correct. A hectare is a square of side 100 m, so 100 × 100 = 10,000 m² — statement 3 is correct. All three hold, so D.

Statement 1 has no basis: the epigram claims that the history of science is the history of mankind — that the two cannot be studied apart — not that mankind could not have survived without science. Statement 2 is actively withheld: the author's point is that science must not be treated 'as some abstract third party', and the passage closes by leaving the question open — 'Is this the inevitable result of the progress of science or does the fault lie elsewhere?' — which is the opposite of emphatically asserting that science determines mankind's destiny. Runner-up is B (2 only): B wins if 'The history of science is the real history of mankind' is read as the author's own endorsement that science drives human destiny, rather than as an epigram he is examining.

items.value: Only assumption 2 is valid — the easily overlooked truth is that science is man's own making
items.reasoning: The passage names the overlooked truth directly: 'it is easy to overlook the relations between science and mankind, and to treat the former as some abstract third party', reinforced by 'Science and mankind cannot be divorced from time to time at men's convenience' — which is exactly assumption 2's point that science is what man has made it. Assumption 1 is not assumed but interrogated: the closing sentence asks whether conflict is 'the inevitable result of the progress of science or does the fault lie elsewhere', and the earlier phrase 'frequently and conveniently blamed' shows the author's scepticism about that blame.

The passage says the travelling merchant comes to know 'what is parochial and what is universal in his choice', and then names the goods concerned — justice, love, honour, courtesy — as values that are 'valid everywhere but … variously moulded'. 'Parochial' versus 'universal' is precisely the local-values-versus-universal-values distinction of option C. Imagination, nationality and friend-or-foe are categories the passage never sets up.

Assumption 2 is near-explicit: 'the art of learning fundamental common values is perhaps the greatest gain of travel'. Assumption 1 follows from the same clause together with its purpose — travel benefits 'those who wish to live at ease among their fellows' — which presupposes that travel deepens understanding of people. Assumption 3 goes further than anything on the page: the passage speaks of the traveller learning to recognise shared values, never of a seasoned traveller resolving disputes between other people. With statement 3 out, only option A remains.

Writing X = 10a + b and Y = 10b + a, the sum is 11(a + b). The greatest two-digit number is 99, which is 11 × 9, so a + b = 9. Both X and Y must be two-digit numbers, so a ≥ 1 and b ≥ 1, leaving (a, b) = (1,8), (2,7), (3,6), (4,5), (5,4), (6,3), (7,2), (8,1) — eight values of X: 18, 27, 36, 45, 54, 63, 72 and 81.

The average weight of the 4 women is 63 kg, so their total weight is 4 × 63 = 252 kg. The chain of equalities gives the total weight of 6 boys as also 252 kg, so the average weight of a boy is 252 ÷ 6 = 42 kg. (The girls and men are surplus information; only the women-to-boys link is needed.)

The hands coincide once every 12/11 hours, i.e. every 65 5/11 minutes. Between 10:00 a.m. and 2:00 p.m. the coincidences fall at approximately 10:54:33 a.m., exactly 12:00 noon, and approximately 1:05:27 p.m. The next one is at about 2:10:54 p.m., which is outside the window, so there are 3 coincidences.

A calendar repeats when the intervening years contribute a whole number of weeks and the leap status matches. The odd days from 2025 to 2030 are 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 (2028 is a leap year) + 1 + 1 = 7 ≡ 0 (mod 7), so 1 January 2031 falls on the same weekday as 1 January 2025 — both Wednesdays — and 2031, like 2025, is not a leap year. The total elapsed days, 2191, is exactly 313 weeks, confirming the repeat.

With p, q odd and r, s even: (1) (p − r) is odd so its square is odd, but qs = odd × even = even, and odd × even is even — correct. (2) (q − s) is odd and q² is odd, but the factor s is even, so the product is even — correct. (3) (q + r) is odd so its square is odd, and (p + s) is odd + even = odd; odd × odd is odd — correct. An exhaustive parity check over distinct odd p, q and even r, s produced no counterexample to any of the three.

The minute hand at 25 minutes stands at 25 × 6 = 150° from 12. The hour hand moves 30° per hour plus 0·5° per minute, so at 4:25 it is at 4 × 30 + 25 × 0·5 = 120 + 12·5 = 132·5°. The angle between them is 150 − 132·5 = 17·5°. (Forgetting the hour hand's 12·5° of drift gives 30°, and forgetting it partly gives the distractors.)

items.value: Only inference 1 holds — the conventional classroom's organising goal is fixed duration rather than competency
items.reasoning: Inference 1 restates the passage's opening claim: 'Conventional classrooms, by emphasizing fixed duration over learning effectiveness, resign themselves to variable outcomes.' Inference 2 overreaches on 'stamp out all differentiation': the passage does describe a one-size-fits-all delivery ('the same set of lectures in the same way for the same duration'), but it says outcomes are precisely NOT undifferentiated — 'a few learners shine, some survive, and the rest are left behind'. Runner-up is C (Both): C wins if 'stamp out all differentiation' is read as failing to differentiate the teaching rather than as erasing differences between learners.

items.value: Neither assumption is valid — both contradict the passage
items.reasoning: Assumption 1 concludes that India need not change the conventional classroom, but the passage's whole argument is that repeating 'the same ineffectual script' will not produce different results. Assumption 2 claims the present system produces enough skilled workers, which the passage flatly denies with '10 percent employability in our graduates after a decade and half of formal education'. The unorganized sector and the demographic dividend are not mentioned at all. Both fail, so D.

items.value: Only assumption 1 is valid — the adolescent is uneasy with parents who are dominating and assertive
items.reasoning: Assumption 1 is carried by two clauses: parental solicitude 'is often a disguise for love of power' (dominating), and the parents' expressed views 'are so dogmatic that the young seldom confide in them, and usually go their own way in secret' (assertive, and the child not at ease). Assumption 2 fails twice over — the passage speaks of secrecy and conflict, never of a lack of respect, and it makes no comparison with adolescents of earlier times, so 'of modern times' is imported. (The passage as printed reads 'The options they express', which appears to be a misprint for 'opinions'; the answer is unaffected either way.)

items.value: Parents may not be of much help while children are becoming adults
items.reasoning: Every element of the passage points this way: conflict is expected at adolescence, the parents' concern masks a love of power, they treat moral questions as their own province, and the result is that 'the young seldom confide in them, and usually go their own way in secret'. That is parents failing to help, which is option A. B overstates it into 'unnecessary', a prescription the author never makes; C introduces nuclear families and D blames the adolescents' character, neither of which appears in the text.

Counting the digit 5 across page numbers 1 to 260: in the units place the numbers 5, 15, …, 255 give 26 occurrences; in the tens place the blocks 50–59, 150–159 and 250–259 give 10 each, or 30; and no page number below 261 has 5 in the hundreds place. The total is 26 + 30 = 56, confirmed by direct enumeration over 1–260.

The sequence falls into blocks of growing length: (1), (1, 2), (1, 3, 2), (1, 4, 3, 2), (1, 5, 4, 3, 2), …, the n-th block having n terms and summing to 1 + (2 + 3 + … + n) = n(n + 1)/2. The blocks use 1 + 2 + … + 7 = 28 terms exactly, so the first 28 terms are the first seven complete blocks and their total is (2 + 6 + 12 + 20 + 30 + 42 + 56)/2 = 168/2 = 84. Direct addition of the 28 listed terms confirms 84.

Let Q cost q. Then R = 1·2q and P = 1·25 × 1·2q = 1·5q, so the total is q + 1·2q + 1·5q = 3·7q = 3,330, giving q = 900. Hence Q = ₹900, R = ₹1,080 and P = ₹1,350. Checking: 1,350 is 25% more than 1,080 and 1,080 is 20% more than 900, and the three sum to ₹3,330.

The equation (10A + B) + (10C + D) = 100 + 10C + E cancels the term 10C on both sides, leaving 10A + B + D = 100 + E. Since B + D can be at most 18 and E is at least 0, 10A ≥ 100 − 18 = 82, forcing A = 9; and A = 9 works, for instance 93 + 28 = 121 with A, B, C, D, E = 9, 3, 2, 8, 1 all distinct. An exhaustive search over distinct digits returns 126 solutions and every one of them has A = 9, so the value is determined even though the other letters are not.

From {1, …, 7}, z = 1 forces 2y > 3, so y ≥ 2. With y = 2, x > 4 gives x = 5, 6 or 7; with y = 3, x > 6 gives x = 7; with y = 4, x > 8 is impossible. For z = 2 we need 2y > 6, so y ≥ 4, and then x > 8, which is out of range; larger z is worse. Exhaustive enumeration over all 343 ordered triplets confirms exactly four.

items.value: Both statements are correct — one orange plus one mango equals one apple in cost, and the two baskets in statement 1 cost the same
items.reasoning: The given condition 4o + 6m + 8a = 2(o + 2m + 5a) simplifies to 2o + 2m − 2a = 0, that is o + m = a, so statement 2 is correct. For statement 1, (4o + 6m + 8a) − (3o + 5m + 9a) = o + m − a, which is zero by the same relation, so the two totals are equal and statement 1 is correct as well.
